requirements.text: The user can run each step of the workflow from chat with a slash command.

origin.quote: I'll drive it from chat with slash commands.

requirements.text: The workflow discovers candidate public GitHub repositories and narrows them to a filtered list of repositories judged worth mining.

origin.quote: Discover candidate repos on GitHub and filter them down to ones worth mining.

requirements.text: Given one chosen repository, the workflow produces a local clone of it checked out at a pinned (fixed, specific) commit.

origin.quote: Pick one repo and clone it at a pinned commit.

requirements.text: For the cloned repository, each commit is enriched with the pull requests and issues that are linked to it.

origin.quote: Enrich its commits with the pull requests and issues linked to them.

requirements.text: The workflow classifies which of the repository's commits are genuine bug fixes, using a subagent to make the classification.

origin.quote: Classify which commits are genuine bug fixes.

requirements.text: Each classification decision is shown to the user together with the evidence behind it, not only a yes or no verdict.

origin.quote: I want to see the evidence for each call, not only a yes or no.

requirements.text: Everything the workflow finds is stored in a local database that persists between runs.

origin.quote: Keep everything in a local database, so I can list past runs and see how many

requirements.text: The user can list past runs.

origin.quote: Keep everything in a local database, so I can list past runs and see how many

requirements.text: For each past run, the user can see how many bug fixes that run found.
The agents in the workflow cannot run arbitrary shell commands.

origin.quote: Don't let the agents run arbitrary shell commands.

requirements.text: Discovery returns only public repositories that are not forks, not archived, and have at least one closed issue or merged pull request.
Discovered repositories are shown ordered by star count, up to the number of results the user asked for (default 10).
The user names the single repository to mine and may give the commit to pin.
When no commit is given, the commit that is current at that moment is pinned and recorded with the run.
Each commit's bug-fix verdict is judged by the subagent from its commit message, its code change and the text of its linked pull request or issue.
Each verdict is stored and shown with a written rationale and quoted excerpts for each of those three kinds of evidence.
The user can limit the scan by a number of commits or a start date; without one, a default limit applies.
Merge commits are not counted among the scanned commits.
Each execution of the pipeline on a repository is stored as one run.
The list of past runs shows one row per run with its repository and the number of bug fixes it found.
When some GitHub lookups fail, the command keeps what it collected, reports each failure to the user and records the run as incomplete.
When GitHub is unreachable or rate-limited, or a repository or commit does not exist, the user is told what failed.
A GitHub token may be read from the environment variables GITHUB_TOKEN or GH_TOKEN and is sent only to GitHub.
The tool does not start another program to obtain a credential.
Without a token the tool continues unauthenticated and tells the user that rate limits are lower.
The launcher may read a token from the project's .env file as plain data but never executes it.
Agents cannot read the .env file.
The tool clones only repositories on github.com, given as owner/repo or a github.com URL.
A repository on any other host, or a local path, is refused with an error and nothing is cloned.

resolvedAmbiguities.question: What makes a discovered repository 'worth mining'?
How is the single repository to mine picked, and how is the pinned commit chosen?
What counts as a 'genuine' bug fix, and what must the evidence for each call contain?
How much history of the repository is enriched and classified?
What is a 'run', and what does the list of past runs show?
What happens on failures such as an unreachable or rate-limited GitHub, a nonexistent repository or commit, or a repository that was already mined?

designNotes.text: The candidate computes the verdict in code from fixed weights; the decision is that the subagent's judgement and rationale decide, so this is recorded as a finding to compare against.

findings.what: With no token found, requests proceed unauthenticated instead of stopping.
findings.why: Requests proceed without a token; lower rate limits are a side effect.

findings.what: Rate limits are retried at most 3 attempts and only if the wait is 90 seconds or less; the process sleeps for the wait.
findings.why: Retry and wait limits are an implementation detail of rate-limit handling.

findings.what: HTTP timeouts are hard-coded at 15 s connect and 30 s per request.
findings.why: Fixed network timeouts are an implementation detail.

findings.what: The launcher starts sbt (compile plus export classpath) when the cached classpath is missing or older than any file in src, build.sbt or project/build.properties, and writes target/causeway.classpath.
findings.why: How the launcher compiles the tool is a launch detail.

findings.what: The launcher changes into the repo root before running, so the relative default data dir resolves under the repo, not the caller's cwd.
findings.why: Which folder the launcher runs from is a launch detail.

findings.what: Data location is controlled by CAUSEWAY_DATA (default `data`).
findings.why: An environment variable chooses the data folder; a configuration detail.

findings.what: The database path can be overridden with CAUSEWAY_DB; default is data/causeway.db.
findings.why: An environment variable chooses the database file; a configuration detail.

findings.what: The SQLite file (and parent directories) is created and the schema applied for every command except help and guard-bash, including an unknown command that then fails.
findings.why: The database is created even for commands that then fail; a side effect.

findings.what: Usage text and errors go to stdout/stderr; a command with no recognised name prints help and exits 0.
findings.why: Help output and its exit code are not mentioned in the prompts.

findings.what: Only UsageError and GitHubError are turned into an error message and exit 1; git, IO and SQL failures propagate as uncaught exceptions.
findings.why: Git, IO and SQL failures end as uncaught exceptions rather than clear messages.

findings.what: Clones are stored at data/repos/<owner>_<repo>, shared by every run of the same repository; the folder is reused without checking its origin against --url.
findings.why: A clone folder is reused for a different --url without checking its origin, so results can silently come from another repository.

findings.what: An existing clone is fetched from origin, pruning deleted refs.
findings.why: Fetching an existing clone is a detail of cloning.

findings.what: The clone's working tree is force-checked-out at the pinned commit, discarding local changes in the clone.
findings.why: The pinned checkout discards local changes in the clone; a detail of how checkout is done.

findings.what: For an existing clone with no branch/commit given, a network ls-remote asks the remote for its HEAD.
findings.why: Asking the remote for its HEAD is a detail of choosing the commit to pin.

findings.what: Stored diffs are cut at 20000 bytes per commit; the classifier is shown only 6000 characters of it.
findings.why: Stored diffs are cut at 20000 bytes and the classifier sees only 6000 characters, so evidence can be based on partial changes.

findings.what: Each candidate costs two extra GitHub search API calls (closed issues, merged PRs).
findings.why: Extra search calls per candidate are an implementation cost.

findings.what: Searching overwrites any earlier stored row for the same repository, including a previous rejection reason.
findings.why: Searching again overwrites an earlier stored row for the same repository, including a previous rejection reason, so stored history is lost.

findings.what: In enrichment, a 404 on an issue/PR lookup is treated as no link rather than an error.
findings.why: A 404 on an issue or PR lookup is treated as no link; an error-handling detail.

findings.what: Only the first page of PRs for a commit is read, and one extra API call is made per distinct referenced number.
findings.why: Only the first page of PRs for a commit is read, so linked pull requests can be missed without notice.

findings.what: Re-running enrich deletes and rewrites the stored links of each commit; PR/issue bodies are cut to 4000 characters.
findings.why: Re-running enrichment rewrites stored links and cuts text at 4000 characters; a storage detail.

findings.what: next-batch silently caps --size at 5.
findings.why: next-batch silently caps --size at 5, so the user gets fewer commits than requested without being told.

findings.what: The reply parser accepts a code fence and an object with a results array, though the agent file forbids fences.
findings.why: The parser tolerates a code fence although the agent file forbids it; a parsing detail.

findings.what: A 'linked' signal supplied for a commit with no links is silently discarded.
findings.why: A linked signal for a commit with no links is dropped; a parsing detail.

findings.what: Valid entries in a reply are stored even when other entries are rejected; rejected ones are only reported.
findings.why: Valid entries in a reply are stored while others are rejected and only reported; a parsing detail.

findings.what: Saving a classification replaces any existing verdict for that commit, and record-classification accepts shas that are already classified.
findings.why: Saving a classification replaces any earlier verdict for the commit, so earlier verdicts and their evidence are lost.

findings.what: The schema is applied by splitting the SQL file on semicolons with comment lines removed, on every open, and foreign keys are enabled per connection.
findings.why: How the schema is applied is an implementation detail.

explainedDiscoveries.reason: Looking up repositories on GitHub is what the discovery step is asked to do.
The guard hook is the mechanism that keeps agents from running arbitrary shell commands, which the prompt asks for.
